title: Acute Asthma Exacerbation
subject: Medicine
summary: An acute worsening of asthma presents with sudden wheeze, breathlessness and cough. Rapid assessment, airway support and bronchodilator therapy are essential, especially in low‑resource settings where investigations may be limited.

sections.p: An acute asthma exacerbation is a sudden increase in symptoms of wheeze, dyspnoea and cough in a patient with known asthma. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by peak flow or spirometry if available.
Severity is staged using the WHO/GINA acute asthma grading: mild, moderate, severe, life‑threatening. Clinical signs guide urgency of treatment.

t.b: Any cyanosis or apnea = urgent referral

sections.p: In East Africa, common triggers include respiratory infections, malaria, HIV, schistosomiasis, herbal remedies, and environmental irritants.

t.b: Positive → treat malaria and monitor asthma

sections.p: Patients report sudden breathlessness, chest tightness, cough, and wheeze. Physical exam shows rapid breathing, use of accessory muscles, and bilateral wheeze.
Investigations are limited in low‑resource settings; focus on clinical assessment and simple tests.
Watch for signs of respiratory failure, pneumothorax, or infection. Complications include pneumonia, pneumothorax, and death if untreated.
b: No breath sounds on one side

sections.p: Treat the trigger, provide bronchodilators, oxygen, and consider steroids. Use available drugs and avoid those with high toxicity.
b: Give inhaled β2‑agonist (salbutamol) via nebuliser or spacer

t.b: Preferred if severe or unresponsive to bronchodilator

sections.p: After stabilization, review inhaler technique, identify and avoid triggers, and ensure adherence to maintenance therapy.

t.b: PEFR > 80% of personal best = good control

whenToSeekHelp: Severe breathlessness with no improvement after 15 min of bronchodilator
No breath sounds on one side

faq.q: What is the first drug to give in an acute asthma attack?
faq.a: An inhaled β2‑agonist such as salbutamol via nebuliser or spacer.

faq.q: Why are systemic steroids used in severe attacks?
faq.a: They reduce airway inflammation and prevent late‑phase bronchoconstriction.

faq.q: Can malaria cause an asthma exacerbation?
faq.a: Yes, malaria can trigger inflammation and worsen asthma; treat both conditions.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with known asthma presents with sudden wheeze and breathlessness. She is using her inhaler but symptoms are worsening. What is the next best step? — Give a nebulised β2‑agonist and assess response; if no improvement, start systemic steroids.
A patient with acute asthma has SpO2 88% on room air. What is the immediate management? — Administer oxygen to target SpO2 > 94% and give a bronchodilator.

A child with asthma presents with wheeze and fever. Chest X‑ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. What is the likely diagnosis? — Pneumonia superimposed on asthma; treat both with antibiotics and bronchodilators.
During an asthma attack, a patient has no breath sounds on the left side. What is the most urgent concern? — Possible pneumothorax; urgent chest X‑ray and decompression if needed.
A patient with asthma is on a β2‑agonist but still has severe symptoms. Which drug class should be added? — Systemic corticosteroids to reduce inflammation.

A patient with asthma in a low‑resource setting cannot get a spirometer. How do you assess severity? — Use clinical signs (accessory muscle use, cyanosis) and peak flow if available; otherwise rely on history and exam.
A patient with asthma has a sudden worsening after taking a herbal remedy. What should you suspect? — The remedy may contain irritants or allergens; consider it a trigger and treat accordingly.
